name: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma
aliases: marginal zone B-cell lymphoma, splenic type

clinicalPearls: An indolent small B-cell lymphoma of marginal-zone origin that involves the spleen, splenic hilar nodes, bone marrow and often the peripheral blood
Typically presents in older adults with splenomegaly, cytopenias from hypersplenism, and villous lymphocytes on the blood film
A recognised association with chronic hepatitis C virus infection exists, and antiviral therapy can induce lymphoma regression in HCV-positive cases
Autoimmune phenomena such as autoimmune haemolytic anaemia or immune thrombocytopenia and a small paraprotein may accompany the disease
The immunophenotype is that of a CD20-positive B cell negative for CD5, CD10, CD23 and cyclin D1, which helps exclude other small B-cell lymphomas
Bone marrow shows a characteristic intrasinusoidal infiltration pattern that is a useful diagnostic clue
Asymptomatic patients may be observed, while symptomatic disease is treated with anti-CD20 targeted therapy, and splenectomy or chemoimmunotherapy in selected cases
reference.pathophysiology: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma arises from a post-germinal-centre memory B cell of the splenic marginal zone. Chronic antigenic stimulation, including that associated with hepatitis C virus infection in a subset of cases, is thought to drive clonal B-cell expansion, and this dependence explains why antiviral therapy can produce regression when HCV is present. The tumour replaces splenic white pulp and infiltrates the red pulp, and typically shows involvement of splenic hilar nodes and an intrasinusoidal pattern in the bone marrow. Recurrent mutations affecting NOTCH2 and the NF-kappaB and marginal-zone differentiation pathways contribute to the neoplastic phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Hairy cell leukaemia and its variant
Nodal or extranodal marginal zone lymphoma with splenic spread
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood film for villous lymphocytes and full blood count for cytopenias
Flow cytometry immunophenotyping showing CD20-positive, CD5/CD10/CD23/cyclin D1-negative B cells
Bone marrow trephine demonstrating intrasinusoidal infiltration
Hepatitis C virus serology and viral load given the therapeutic implications
Serum protein electrophoresis and immunoglobulins for a paraprotein
Direct antiglobulin test and haemolysis markers if anaemia is present
Imaging to characterise splenomegaly and exclude bulky nodal disease
redFlags: Rapid splenic enlargement, new B symptoms or rising lactate dehydrogenase suggesting transformation to aggressive lymphoma
Severe cytopenias causing bleeding or infection risk
Symptomatic autoimmune haemolysis or immune thrombocytopenia
Splenic rupture or infarction from massive splenomegaly
reference.prognosis: Most patients follow an indolent course with prolonged survival, and HCV-associated cases may regress with antiviral therapy; adverse outcomes are associated with transformation to aggressive large B-cell lymphoma and with certain molecular features such as TP53 abnormalities.
pitfalls: Failing to test for hepatitis C virus and missing a case treatable with antiviral therapy
Confusing the disease with hairy cell leukaemia or chronic lymphocytic leukaemia without full immunophenotyping
Overlooking the intrasinusoidal bone marrow pattern that supports the diagnosis
Attributing cytopenias solely to marrow infiltration when hypersplenism or autoimmunity is responsible
Missing transformation in a patient with sudden clinical change
references: British Society for Haematology guidance on marginal zone lymphomas
management: Almost all patients present with stage IV disease due to marrow and blood involvement, so treatment is driven by symptom burden rather than stage.
Asymptomatic patients without splenomegaly or cytopenias can be observed rather than treated immediately.
Treatment is indicated once symptomatic splenomegaly and/or significant cytopenias develop.
In hepatitis C-associated disease, antiviral treatment of the infection is a reasonable first step, as it has been shown to induce regression of the lymphoma.
Splenectomy is a reasonable option for selected patients needing treatment and can provide excellent relief of symptoms and cytopenias.
Splenic radiotherapy has some utility for patients who are not surgical candidates, with the dose kept under renal tolerance since the left kidney is usually in the treatment field.
Single-agent anti-CD20 antibody therapy (rituximab) can improve splenomegaly and cytopenias in most patients.
Relapse options include retreatment with an anti-CD20 antibody, alkylating agents, and purine analogs combined with an anti-CD20 antibody.
A Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor (ibrutinib) is also an option at relapse.

More broadly for marginal zone lymphomas as a group, Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors and PI3K-pathway inhibitors have shown activity in relapsed disease, and CD19-directed CAR T-cell therapy is being explored in later lines; these are extrapolated from marginal zone lymphoma biology rather than splenic-specific evidence.
Monitor blood counts and clinical status (spleen size, cytopenias, constitutional symptoms) for disease progression.
Watch for signs of histologic transformation to a more aggressive lymphoma, such as rapid change in nodal or splenic size, new B symptoms, or a rising lactate dehydrogenase.
Refer to haemato-oncology for diagnostic confirmation, hepatitis C testing and hepatology coordination if positive, and decisions between splenectomy, splenic radiotherapy, or systemic therapy.
Refer urgently for signs of transformation, severe cytopenias, or splenic complications such as rupture or infarction.
